source: NCERT Democratic Politics II (Class X Political Science), Chapter 3

overview.bigIdea: Social differences need not threaten democracy. **Gender** shows a division that *should* be raised in politics; **religion** shows how politics can turn dangerous (communalism); **caste** shows both good and bad sides.

lessons.title: Gender and politics
lessons.hook: ‘My mother says she doesn’t work – she is a housewife. But she works non-stop!’ This is the **sexual division of labour**: women’s work at home is unpaid, unseen and not counted – and it keeps women out of public life.

core.def: A hierarchical social division based not on biology but on social expectations and stereotypes.
All work inside the home is done or organised by women; men work outside. When paid, men do these jobs too (tailors, cooks).
Women’s movements for equality in voting rights, education, careers and even personal and family life.
Literally rule by father – a system that values men more and gives them power over women.
Literacy 54% (women) vs 76% (men) · lower pay despite the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 · child sex ratio 919 · violence and harassment.

explain: **Representation:** women in the Lok Sabha touched 14.36% for the first time in 2019; less than 5% in State assemblies. One-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities are reserved – more than 10 lakh women representatives. The **Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023** will give 33% reservation in the Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and Delhi Assembly.
**Why it matters:** unless women control power, their problems will not get adequate attention. Gender division is an example that some social divisions *need* to be expressed in politics.

example.q: Mention different aspects of life in which women are discriminated against or disadvantaged in India. (5 marks)
steps: **Education:** female literacy is 54% compared with 76% for men; fewer girls go for higher studies.
**Work and pay:** women’s household work is unpaid; they are paid less than men for the same work despite the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976.
**Jobs:** a very small proportion of women hold highly paid and valued jobs.
**Sex ratio:** sex-selective abortion has lowered the child sex ratio to 919 girls per 1000 boys.
**Safety:** harassment, exploitation, domestic violence; urban areas are particularly unsafe.
example.answer: Education, pay, jobs, sex ratio, safety – five points with data.

mistakes: Writing that one-third reservation already applies to the Lok Sabha as current practice (it is in local bodies; the 2023 Act provides for the legislatures).
lessons.tip: In any women’s-representation answer, write BOTH the problem (14.36%, <5%) and the solution (1/3 in local bodies, 2023 Act).
lessons.memory: Literacy 54–76 · Lok Sabha 14.36 · Sex ratio 919 · Law 1976 · Act 2023.

lessons.title: Religion, communalism and politics
lessons.hook: Religion in politics is not always wrong – Gandhiji said politics must be guided by the moral values of religion. The problem starts when **one religion is set against another** and state power is used for one group’s domination. That is **communalism**.

core.def: People may express needs as members of a religious community; ideas from religions can guide politics; the state may regulate religion to stop discrimination – as long as every religion is treated equally.
Based on the idea that religion is the principal basis of social community: followers of one religion form one community with the same interests, different from others.

1 Everyday beliefs: prejudices, stereotypes. 2 Quest for political dominance (majoritarian dominance or separate political unit). 3 Political mobilisation on religious lines. 4 Communal violence, riots, massacre.
No official religion · freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion or none · no discrimination on grounds of religion · state can intervene to ensure equality (bans untouchability).

explain: Communalism is flawed because people of one religion do not have the same interests everywhere; everyone has many identities and there are many voices in every community.
A secular Constitution is **necessary but not sufficient**: communal prejudices must be countered in everyday life and religion-based mobilisation in politics.

example.q: State different forms of communal politics with one example each. (5 marks)
steps: **Everyday beliefs:** religious prejudices, stereotypes and belief in the superiority of one’s religion – e.g. jokes stereotyping a community.
**Political dominance:** majoritarian dominance for the majority, or a desire for a separate political unit for a minority.
**Mobilisation on religious lines:** use of sacred symbols, religious leaders, emotional appeals and fear to win votes.
**Communal violence:** riots and massacres – e.g. at the time of Partition.
Conclusion: communalism threatens the very idea of India, so it must be combated.
example.answer: Four forms, each with an example, plus a conclusion.

mistakes: Calling any mention of religion in politics ‘communal’.
Saying India’s Constitution keeps the state completely away from religion – it can intervene for equality.
Forgetting that communalism affects the majority too.
lessons.tip: Learn the four forms in order of seriousness: Beliefs → Dominance → Mobilisation → Violence.

Communal – people have many identities.

lessons.title: Caste and politics
lessons.hook: Caste is special to India: hereditary occupations sanctioned by rituals. It has changed hugely – yet it has not disappeared. In politics it works **both ways**: caste affects politics, and politics changes caste.

core.def: Hereditary occupational division sanctioned by rituals; members married within the group and excluded ‘outcaste’ groups (untouchability).

Efforts of reformers (Jotiba Phule, Gandhiji, B.R. Ambedkar, Periyar), economic development, urbanisation, literacy, occupational mobility, weaker landlords; the Constitution prohibits caste discrimination.
Parties choose candidates by caste composition · governments include different castes · appeals to caste sentiment · universal adult franchise made leaders mobilise all castes.
Caste groups grow by incorporating sub-castes · form coalitions and negotiate · new groups like ‘backward’ and ‘forward’ castes.
SC 16.6% and ST 8.6% (Census 2011); OBC about 41% (NSS 2004–05). Poverty is highest among ST and SC and lowest among upper castes.

explain: **Elections are not only about caste:** no constituency has a clear majority of one caste; no party gets all votes of a caste; several parties may field candidates of the same caste; ruling parties often lose; voters’ attachment to parties and assessment of performance matter.
**Both sides:** caste politics helped Dalits and OBCs gain access to decision making; but exclusive attention to caste can divert attention from poverty, development and corruption and cause tension.

example.q: State two reasons to say that caste alone cannot determine election results in India. (3 marks)
steps: No parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one single caste, so every candidate needs the support of more than one caste.
No party wins the votes of all voters of a caste; rich and poor, men and women of the same caste often vote differently.
The ruling party and sitting MPs/MLAs frequently lose – impossible if castes were frozen in their preferences; performance of governments matters.
example.answer: Mixed constituencies · divided caste votes · performance matters.

mistakes: Mixing up caste in politics and politics in caste.
Writing only negatives – examiners want both sides.
lessons.tip: ‘Caste in politics’ = what caste DOES to politics. ‘Politics in caste’ = what politics DOES to caste.
lessons.memory: Caste in politics → candidates, cabinets, campaigns. Politics in caste → grow, ally, new groups.
examAsk: How are caste inequalities still continuing?

revision: Gender division is social, not biological; sexual division of labour keeps women’s work unpaid and invisible.
Feminist movements demanded equal political, legal, educational, career and family rights.
Women’s literacy 54% vs men 76%; child sex ratio 919; Equal Remuneration Act 1976; women work 1 hour more daily.
Women in Lok Sabha 14.36% (2019), assemblies <5%; 1/3 seats in local bodies (10 lakh+ women); 2023 Act: 33% in Lok Sabha, Assemblies, Delhi.
Gandhiji: religion (moral values) cannot be separated from politics.
Communalism: religion as the principal basis of community; four forms – beliefs, dominance, mobilisation, violence.
Secular state: no official religion; freedom of religion; no discrimination; state intervenes for equality.
Caste: hereditary occupations sanctioned by rituals; weakened by reformers, urbanisation, literacy, mobility.
SC 16.6%, ST 8.6%, OBC ~41%; caste still linked to economic status.
Caste in politics (candidates, cabinets, appeals) vs politics in caste (grow, ally, new groups); both positive and negative effects.

sections.title: Social-division answers · 4 steps
items: Define the division (gender / communalism / casteism).
Give the forms or facts in points.
Add data from the chapter.
End with a balanced judgement (positive and negative in politics).

sections.title: Answer writing that scores
items: Start with a one-line definition or introduction using textbook keywords (e.g. ‘Majoritarianism is …’).
Write in points – one idea per point, with the key term in the first few words. A 3-mark answer needs 3 clear points; a 5-mark answer needs 5.
Add a real example from the chapter to each point (Belgium, Sri Lanka, Panchayati Raj, a party, a survey figure).
Use the exact numbers the textbook gives only when you are sure (59%, 1956, 1992, one-third, 1976).
For ‘Explain / Analyse’ questions use PEE: Point → Explain → Example. For ‘Distinguish’ questions draw a small two-column table.
Case-based questions: underline the key line in the passage first; the answer is usually hidden in it.

sections.title: Before the exam
items: Revise the key facts sheet and the revision list the night before.
Redo the Play & learn sorts – if you can sort every card first time, you know the chapter.
Practise one 5-mark answer in 8–10 minutes with a timer.

checklist: I can explain the sexual division of labour and feminist movements.
I can give five ways women are disadvantaged, with data.
I can state women’s representation and the reservation provisions.
I can list four forms of communalism and four secular provisions.
I can explain caste in politics and politics in caste with both effects.
exam.paperNote: Based on the CBSE Class X Social Science pattern (MCQ, assertion–reason, 3-mark short, 4-mark case/source-based and 5-mark long answers). Practise these types first.

method: Built on proven learning methods: understand the story first, sort and match ideas with your hands (active learning), write model answers point by point, test yourself (active recall) and revisit after 1, 3 and 7 days (spaced revision).
